newsitem.title: INDIA: India gives Rio, BHP aerial survey rights.
newsitem.headline: India gives Rio, BHP aerial survey rights.

text.p: India has granted Australia's Rio Tinto Plc /Ltd and Broken Hill Pty Co airborne survey prospecting rights in the northwestern state of Rajasthan, a senior state government official said.

S.P. Gupta, energy and mines secretary in the Rajasthan government, told Reuters in an interview at the weekend that Britain's Metdist Group and Canada's Meridian Peak Resources Corp had also been permitted to aerially prospect in the state.
"The multinational companies will undertake airborne surveys in a total area of over 20,000 sq km in Rajasthan state," Gupta said.
"These surveys would be of base metals and associated minerals and the companies are likely to invest $100 million in all in the surveys."
Rio Tinto, formerly RTZ Corp Plc-CRA Ltd, and the three other firms will undertake the surveys through their Indian subsidiaries, Gupta said.
CRA Exploration (India) Pvt Ltd, which has signed an agreement with India's leading cement firm Associated Cement Co Ltd (ACC), will undertake airborne surveys over an area of 2,432.52 sq km.
BHP Minerals, in partnership with state-run Hindustan Zinc Ltd, has been allotted an area of 18,169 sq km for prospecting base metals, noble metals and associated minerals.

BHP Minerals has already started prospecting, Gupta said. The firm will spend $10 million in airborne surveys for lead, zinc, copper, gold and associated minerals in six districts of Rajasthan state, he said.

Metmin Finance and Holdings, the Bombay-based subsidiary of Metdist, will prospect over an area of 2,517.67 sq km. Metmin has also been given two ground prospecting licences across an area of 23 sq km.

Meridian's Indian subsidiary Meridian Minerals India Pvt Ltd has been given an aerial survey prospecting licence for an area of 1,303 sq km in the districts of Banswara and Bharatpur. Meridian will survey base and noble metals, Gupta said.

The Indian mining sector, which was liberalised in 1996, has already attracted investment worth $278 million. Foreign firms can hold up to 50 percent of mining companies' equity in India, and even up to 100 percent in specific cases.

"Rajasthan has the largest potential belt of base metals in the country, extending for a length of 260 km (155 miles). The state has about 400 million tonnes of identified reserves of lead-zinc ore with 15 percent lead and 14.5 percent zinc," state chief minister Bhairon Singh Shekhawat told Reuters.
"About 165 million tonnes of copper ore reserves are also there to be explored," Shekhawat said.
Multiple prospecting and exploration of minerals are allowed on leased land in various parts of the country, Gupta said.

"The multinationals are making a beeline with mining equipment manufacturing companies to meet the demands of mechanised mining," he said. "The mine sector is bound to grow leaps and bounds in coming years."
